noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms
noteRef.subtopicTitle: Movement of Substances into and out of Cells

specPoints.text: understand how factors affect the rate of movement of substances into and out of cells, including the effects of surface area to volume ratio, distance, temperature and concentration gradient

primer.text: You already know that substances slip into and out of cells by diffusion, and that the distance between two points matters. This lesson turns that intuition into the four measurable factors — the surface-to-volume balance, the travel distance, the warmth, and the gradient's steepness — that set the speed of exchange in any cell.

lessons.title: Four Factors That Set the Rate
lessons.opening: The speed at which oxygen, carbon dioxide and other substances cross cell boundaries is not fixed — four factors set it. A larger surface spread over a given volume speeds exchange, a shorter distance helps, warmer particles move faster, and a steeper concentration difference pushes harder. Big organisms answer the surface problem with special exchange surfaces.
keyPoints: As a cell or organism grows larger, its surface area to volume ratio falls.
Specialised exchange surfaces such as alveoli and villi restore the area lost to size.
Root hair cells and ileum lining cells show surface-increasing adaptations.
The shorter the distance molecules must travel, the faster diffusion completes.
Higher temperature raises kinetic energy, so particles cross the membrane sooner.
A steeper concentration difference across the membrane speeds the crossing.

low.restatement: More area, less distance, more heat, bigger gap: all four speed diffusion up.
low.analogy: A wide, short, warm slide between two crowded and empty rooms.
low.examPointer: Learn the four factors as a list — questions ask you to name them all.

medium.restatement: Each factor works through collision geometry: area sets how many doors, distance the corridor length, temperature the walking speed, gradient the crowd pressure.
medium.analogy: Shoppers entering a mall through many wide doors on a cold-short path during a sale.
medium.examPointer: Link each factor to one named adaptation — folded intestine, one-cell-thick walls.

check.stem: What happens to surface area to volume ratio as an organism grows larger?

options.text: It decreases, leaving less exchange surface per unit of volume
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: It increases, easing exchange
options.explanation: Volume grows faster than surface area, so the ratio falls.

options.text: It stays constant at all sizes
options.explanation: The two scale differently, so the ratio changes.

options.text: It doubles with every size doubling
options.explanation: No such fixed doubling exists.

check.stem: Why do larger organisms evolve specialised exchange surfaces?

options.text: To raise the surface area available for diffusion despite their low surface area to volume ratio
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: To shorten their digestion time
options.explanation: Exchange surfaces serve diffusion, not digestion speed.

options.text: To reduce their overall volume
options.explanation: The volume stays; the surface is what is increased.

options.text: To eliminate the need for blood supply
options.explanation: Good blood supply accompanies these surfaces.

check.stem: Which adaptation is cited for cells specialised for diffusion?

options.text: Increased surface area, as in root hair cells and ileum lining cells
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Thicker walls to slow escape
options.explanation: Thicker walls would slow crossing, not speed it.

options.text: Fewer organelles to make room
options.explanation: Space inside the cell is not the limiting factor.

options.text: Lower temperature inside the cell
options.explanation: Cooler particles move more slowly.

check.stem: How does temperature raise the rate of movement across a membrane?

options.text: Warmer particles carry more kinetic energy and strike the membrane more often
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Warmth widens the membrane's pores
options.explanation: The membrane does not open pores when heated.

options.text: Warmth dissolves the membrane
options.explanation: The membrane stays intact across the normal range.

options.text: Warmth increases the concentration gradient
options.explanation: Gradient is a separate factor.

check.stem: Why does a steeper concentration gradient speed up exchange?

options.text: More particles sit on the crowded side, so more random collisions send them across
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Particles gain energy from the gradient
options.explanation: The gradient adds no energy; it adds pressure of numbers.

options.text: The membrane opens wider for steep gradients
options.explanation: Membrane permeability is independent of gradient.

options.text: Steep gradients shorten the diffusion distance
options.explanation: Distance is governed by wall thickness, not gradient.

check.stem: Name the four factors that influence the rate of movement of substances.
check.modelAnswer: The surface-to-volume balance, the travel distance, the temperature, and the gradient's steepness.

check.stem: State why alveoli and capillary walls are one cell thick.
check.modelAnswer: To keep the diffusion distance minimal so gases cross rapidly between air and blood.

check.stem: Explain why a highly folded surface, such as the intestine lining, speeds absorption.
check.modelAnswer: Folding packs far more membrane into the same space, which raises the surface area available for diffusion; with more area, more particles can cross at the same moment, so absorption proceeds faster per unit of volume.

check.stem: A single-celled pond organism and a large mammal exchange substances with their surroundings. Explain why only one needs specialised exchange organs.
check.modelAnswer: The pond cell is small, so its surface area to volume ratio stays high and plain diffusion supplies it; the mammal is large, its ratio is low, so it needs surfaces such as alveoli with rich blood supply to restore exchange speed.

glossary.definition: The comparison between exchange surface and body volume; it falls as size grows.
How far particles must travel to cross an exchange boundary; shorter is faster.
A specialised area, such as alveoli or villi, where diffusion happens at high rate.
